Wake: send a magic packet — configure the MAC and enable Wake-on-LAN in the BIOS.
Sleep: suspend to RAM; the web service stops — the computer shows offline until woken (needs MAC and WoL).
Shut down: powers off immediately; the web service stops — afterwards only Wake works (needs MAC) or the physical power button.
Restart: reboots immediately; the web session drops — it comes back online automatically after reboot.
Without a power route it calls this computer\'s own /api/power (must be reachable); with a route it sends a LAN SOL packet.

Drag ☰ (or click ↑↓) to reorder; probes and API requests try channels in this order, using the first that works. Each channel can set its own timeout: 1–2 s is enough on a LAN, while public Funnel/built-in Funnel may need 5–8 s for the first handshake. A blank cell uses the default below.
How to probe the priority channels (how the six channels are tried; applies to every channel above)

Probing on the computer page and list follows this: Parallel (first) fires all channels at once and uses the first success; Parallel (all) waits for all and reports each channel\'s result and time; Serial tries channels in the priority order and stops at the first success. This is channel-level; the “multi-NIC probe” below is address-level within one channel. Probes run on a separate thread pool, so larger timeouts or Parallel (all) won\'t freeze the UI.
Per-block strategy (how multiple entries in one block are probed) + block default timeout
This block\'s default probe timeout (s); blank = global default

Per block: Parallel (first) stops at the first hit and marks the rest “not probed” (fast); Parallel (all) reports each entry (for health checks); Serial tries in row order and stops at the first success (strict priority). Under Parallel (first), order only affects launch order — earlier rows don\'t always win; choose Serial for strict order. Block default timeout applies to rows without their own; if blank, the global default below is used.
Multi-NIC probe (how multiple addresses within one channel are probed)

Applies when a computer has multiple LAN addresses (multiple NICs / changed IPs): Parallel (first) uses whichever works first; Parallel (all) waits for all; Serial tries in address order and stops at the first success.
Default probe timeout (s) — used when a channel cell is blank
Default 2 s (range 0.2–30 s). To wait longer/shorter for a channel, fill that row\'s cell — a filled cell wins; blank cells use this default.
Jump hosts are per address — each “LAN address” row above has its own jump-host dropdown; empty = direct. With three NICs you can relay each via home/office jump hosts independently.

Calls this computer\'s own /api/power (token shared with the connection; no extra config). Mixed = send HTTP and magic packet together.

With routes configured, power buttons send UDP packets on the LAN and the computer\'s sol performs the action by port — works while asleep or disconnected; without routes, wake uses standard WOL. Blank broadcast = auto (global broadcast + /24 of each address).

A pairing code = this computer\'s tunnel address + a dedicated token; one per client, revocable individually. It can be generated even when the channel is off (tunnel address blank, filled in by the client). A quick tunnel changes address on every app restart — old records can still reconcile: if the client\'s “last seen” is later than the address change, it\'s using the new address; if it never updates, it\'s still on the old one (or not connected). The pairing string is shown only once (the server stores a hash only) — if scanning fails or the peer deleted it, click “Reissue” in the list below to get a new token and rescan; no need to re-add.
No paired clients yet — click “Generate pairing code” to send a token to a phone or another computer.

After saving, each section\'s pairings probe independently and time separately; clearing all and saving unpairs. A pairing code is like a password — don\'t forward it.
Connection priority (↑↓ to reorder; end toggle enable/disable; the small box under the name = this route\'s own probe timeout in s, blank = default below)

Probe and API requests try each route in this order; the first that works is used. Each route can set its own probe timeout (LAN 1–2 s is fine; public-relay Funnel / built-in Funnel handshake is slow at first — give 5–8 s). Pick the jump host profile below first; power wake doesn\'t follow this order — a magic packet only broadcasts on the LAN.
Probe mode for connection priority (how the six routes are tried; applies to each route above)

Parallel·first: fire all routes at once, use whichever succeeds first; Parallel·all: wait for all and report each route\'s result and time; Serial: try in the priority order, stop at the first that works.
Multi-NIC probe (how multiple addresses within a route are tried)
Applies when a computer has multiple LAN addresses (several NICs / IP changed by DHCP): parallel uses whichever works first; serial tries in order.
Within-section strategy (how pairings in a section are tried) and the section default timeout

Parallel·first: all in the section fire at once, the first to succeed may not be the top row; Serial: strictly by row order within the section. Each pairing can set another timeout on its own row (item → section → global default).
